Counts are in the section files.
11	- **Decisions it does not appear to agree with**: named with the owner's words (compared with `records/Semantics - Decisions.md`). **FLAGGED** = at least one, for Part C. Where the owner's own case turns on a reading the owner has not settled, the flag holds **"on that reading"** only; the reading is the owner's (rule 12).
12	- **The owner's cases**: S44's case is the two-part sign (a red part that switches on on Mondays and a blue part on Tuesdays); the one-part sign is the program's companion case.
13	- **Against Part A's list (C1–C21)**: where a Part B candidate admits and drops the same as a Part A candidate on every case computed, it is said; the comparison runs are in `computation/comparisons with Part A/` (each case computed in both programs).
14	
15	## 1. The candidates
16	
17	| # | variant (free item) | statement: being an explanation with it on | admits (computed) | drops (computed) | the owner's four cases | decisions it does not appear to agree with | flag | Part A |
18	|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|

21	| PB-C3 | PB1.3 (D3.2, R2V1.8) | a query whose answers are not values of the designated port names no question | none | the pole's identification question C_id | all stay | none found | – | none |
22	| PB-C4 | PB1.6 (L103.s1, D1.3) | deleting a part empties it (not frees it), so a part idle for the answer can still carry the dependence | 61 generated; the reply's idle-commitment case | none | all stay | none found | – | none |

24	| PB-C6 | PB2.1 (L189.s2, R2V2.7) | "faithful" includes answering the question right, so a link picked by trial that answers wrong where it was tried is not selected but declared | none | FC104.new1 (b)'s selected transport (declared, so no explanation there) | all stay (the bridge's holding is by hand) | none found | – | none |
25	| PB-C7 | PB2.2 (D5.5) | the link need not respect how changes combine, only match state by state | the reversed calculation of the pole under τ′ on C1; 11 generated; the relabeling candidate on a selection history | none | all stay | none found | – | none |
26	| PB-C8 | PB2.3 (D5.4) | every part of the candidate, not only the parts offered as doing the work, must match the thing's parts | none | 214 generated (mostly candidates with a background part with no counterpart: S109-B2-I1 decides it) | all stay | none found | – | none |

31	| PB-C13 | PB3.3 (L195.s1, s5) | a link picked by trial counts as picked only if it was tried on every pair of the question that has occurred | none | on the hand-set selection history (every pair of C occurred, only the baseline tried): every explanation, 44 of 49 cases, 999 generated | on a selection history: the two-part sign and the vane stop being explanations (every encoding); with a worked-out link they stay | **S41 Q2** ("No, not if just declared"; Claude's question set a link "simply declared" against one "found by trial or worked out": here one found by trial counts as declared); **S44** and **S41 Q15**, on a selection history | **FLAGGED** | nearest **C16**: both drop every explanation on the hand-set selection history; they part on the claims (FC77, FC104.new1 move under C16 only; FC83, FC12.new1's parts under PB-C13 only), so not the same on every case computed |
32	| PB-C14 | PB3.4 (L199.s1, s3) | a link is declared only if no holding of it anywhere was found or worked out | the student's copy; 82 of 584 chain outputs | none | the student's copy becomes an explanation; the bridge stays | **S41 Q2** ("No, not if just declared") | **FLAGGED** | none (C21, C12 differ on CT8 and the chains) |
33	| PB-C15 | PB3.6 (D11.1, L169.s1) | only what lies inside the system's own boundary counts in its history | on that reading (the textbook outside the student's boundary), the student's copy with one pair tried | none | the student's copy becomes an explanation, on that reading, where the student tried one pair | **S41 Q2** ("No, not if just declared"), **on that reading** | **FLAGGED** (on that reading) | none |
34	
35	Same axis across the parts (for the owner, not a ranking): PB-C9, PB-C10 with Part A's C6, C11 (the written-in answer); PB-C11, PB-C14, PB-C15 with C7, C12, C21 (a declared copy); PB-C13 with C16 (a found link counted as declared); PB-C2, PB-C3, PB-C5 with C2, C15 (whether a question is a question); PB-C5 with C5 (a change made to the thing).
36	
37	## 2. For the owner: the flagged candidates in plain words
38	
39	Each: one sentence, an everyday example, and the past decision it seems to go against, in the owner's words.
40	
41	**PB-C2.** *In one sentence:* a question only counts if every change it asks about is one the world could actually bring about. *Example:* "why would this bridge sag if its steel were twice as heavy?" asks about a change nobody can make to that bridge, so on this reading nothing answers it. On the reading that the changes in your cases cannot be made to the thing, your two-part sign and your weathervane explanations stop counting; if the day and the wind are read as circumstances rather than changes, nothing moves. *Seems to go against* S25: "It has nothing to do with explanation."; and, on that reading, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation." and S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained".
42	
43	**PB-C5.** *In one sentence:* a question must ask about at least one change made to the thing itself, not only about different circumstances around it. *Example:* "why is the lamp on when I flip the switch?" counts; "why is the lamp on at night and off at noon?" alone does not. On the reading that Tuesday and the north wind are circumstances of your sign and your vane, not changes made to them, neither your two-part sign explanation nor the vane's counts; on the reading that they are changes, nothing moves. *Seems to go against*, on that reading, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation." and S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained".
44	
45	**PB-C9.** *In one sentence:* if some background part of a candidate simply fixes the answer, the candidate is not an explanation at all. *Example:* a recipe card that explains why the cake is sweet by listing the steps, with a note tucked in the back saying "result: sweet", stops counting. *Seems to go against* S45: "Yes, take the test out".
46	
47	**PB-C10.** *In one sentence:* a candidate whose answer is simply written into one of its parts fails the test of answering the question, so it is not an explanation. *Example:* a table listing "Monday: red, Tuesday: blue" as its only part stops counting. Your two-part sign stays one on the reading that a part is "written in" only if it alone gives the answer everywhere asked; on the other readings it stops being one. *Seems to go against* S45: "Yes, take the test out"; and, on those readings, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation."
48	
49	**PB-C11.** *In one sentence:* a copy of a whole worked-out result counts as worked out too. *Example:* the student who copies the pendulum formula from a textbook and writes "this stands for the pendulum" has an explanation, because the textbook's author worked it out. *Seems to go against* S41 Q2: "No, not if just declared".
50	
51	**PB-C13.** *In one sentence:* a link picked by trial counts as picked only if it was tried on every case of the question that has come up; otherwise it counts as simply declared. *Example:* a gardener who kept the watering schedule that worked in spring, though summer had already come round once, has only declared it. An explanation of your sign or your vane reached by trying and keeping what worked, where not every day or wind that came up was tried, would stop being an explanation. *Seems to go against* S41 Q2: "No, not if just declared" (Claude's question set a link "simply declared" against one "found by trial or worked out"); and, for such a history, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation." and S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained".
52	
53	**PB-C14.** *In one sentence:* a link counts as found or worked out if anyone who ever held it found or worked it out. *Example:* the student copying the pendulum formula holds the same link the author worked out, so the student has an explanation. *Seems to go against* S41 Q2: "No, not if just declared".
54	
55	**PB-C15.** *In one sentence:* only what happened inside the student's own reach counts in the story of the student's link. *Example:* the textbook sits outside the student's boundary, so the student who checked the copied formula on one swing counts as having found it by trial (on the reading that the textbook is outside that boundary). *Seems to go against*, on that reading, S41 Q2: "No, not if just declared".
56	
57	## 3. Not in the list
58	
59	- **Implemented, changing neither which candidates meet (E) nor which are explanations**: PB1.4, PB1.8, PB1.9 (kinds: FC04, FC05, FC16, FC103.new1 move), PB1.5 (Found; no reader), PB2.4 ((A) over determined pairs: meaning moves, no candidate enters; FC21, FC96, FC109 move), PB2.8, PB2.9 (no code change), PB3.5 (meaning only), PB3.7 (New), PB4.1, PB4.2, PB4.3, PB4.4′, PB4.5 to PB4.8 (ruling out, the defeat sets, criticism, problems, the class's list).
60	- **Recorded for the orchestrator, not flagged as candidates** (they sit against an owner's decision as the computation shows it, but change no explanation): **PB4.1** (a premise alone no longer rules out the design: FC72 (d), FC72.new1 (c)) against **S41 Q23** ("Yes, it's an argument") with **S28** ("That "ruling out" is a choice that was made."); **PB4.4′** (no argument is usable until its premises' explanations are held, so nothing is ruled out) against **S27** ("the creative agent need not contain the entirety of why perpetual motion is impossible."); **PB4.8** (a problem stands whether or not the person has ruled a rival out) against **S21** ("Resolution is up to the person and the person's choice.").
61	- **Flagged out, not computed**: PB3.8 (no formal statement); PB4.4 as written (computed as PB4.4′ on D9.8).
62	- **Not taken up**: R2V1.2 (class b).
63	
64	## 4. Gaps (rule 10)
65	
66	The map's §5: gaps remain that a round 2 of Part B could reach (D1.1's and D1.2's clauses, L147.s1–s2, D5.2, D6.1, L169.s2; four edges left claimed only). A proposal; the settlement after the GLM cross-examination decides round 2 of Part B or Part C.
67	
68	## 5. Unsure
69	
70	- The decisions named are this agent's reading of the owner's words against the computed effect; each FLAG says only that the candidate does not appear to agree (S52). S41's questions are Claude's; only the owner's chosen answers are quoted as the owner's.
71	- PB-C2's S25 flag reads "what counts as an explanation … must not be defined by physical possibility" (Claude's reading of S25) as reached by a question-defining clause; the owner's S26 ("Well not strictly nothing") keeps physical possibility where something is instantiated.
72	- PB-C13's drops rest on the hand-set selection history, in which every pair of the contract occurs and only the baseline was tried (I90); on a history where only tried pairs occurred nothing moves.
73	- PB-C8's drops rest mostly on S109-B2-I1 (a background part with no counterpart fails); with such parts exempt, few or none would drop.
74	- The everyday examples are this agent's, written to show the sentence, not computed cases; the owner's own cases are the computed ones.
75	- Nothing here says what hard to vary covers (S33, S34), what must happen to candidates (S21), or which candidate to prefer (S20).
76	
77	Written by one Opus 5.5 agent under rule 7 and decision S56, 29 September 2026. Nothing applied (rule 13).

## 4. For the owner: the flagged candidates in plain words

Each: one sentence, an everyday example, and the past decision it seems to go against, in the owner's words.

**C1.** *In one sentence:* each part of an explanation has to match what its piece of the thing does inside the whole, not the rule that piece follows on its own. *Example:* a bicycle's gear part may only say "the wheel turns at the speed it turns now with this rider", not "the gears multiply whatever the pedals do". On your shop sign, the red-part and blue-part explanation would no longer be an explanation, however the change of day is read. *Seems to go against* S44: "In either case, it is an explanation."

**C2.** *In one sentence:* only a question that was itself found or worked out can be answered; a question simply laid down has no answer. *Example:* a customer just asks "why is the sign red on Mondays?", with no story of how the question arose; on the reading that such a question counts as laid down, nothing explains the sign or the weathervane. Your engineer's bridge is touched only on further readings: that the work included criticizing a first design, and that "creating" is taken in the program's narrow sense; then nothing counts as created there. Without a criticized first design, nothing counted as created there before either, so nothing changes. Where the question's story is recorded as found or worked out, nothing changes. [Xd1] *Seems to go against*, on that reading, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation."; S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained"; S41 Q6: "Yes, it can".

**C5.** *In one sentence:* a difference counts towards an explanation only when it comes with a change made to the thing, not from its circumstances. *Example:* "because someone flipped the switch" can explain a lamp being on; "because it is night" cannot. On the reading that the north wind and the day of the week are circumstances of the vane and the sign, nothing explains why the vane points north, and your two-part sign explanation is not one; on the reading that they are changes made to them, nothing changes. *Seems to go against*, on that reading, S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained", and S44: "In either case, it is an explanation."

**C6.** *In one sentence:* something whose answer is simply written into one of its parts is not an explanation at all. *Example:* a table that just lists the answers stops being an explanation. Your red-part and blue-part sign stays one on the reading that a part is "written in" only if it alone gives the answer everywhere asked; on the readings where giving it somewhere is enough, it stops being one. *Seems to go against* S45: "Yes, take the test out"; and, on those readings, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation."

**C7.** *In one sentence:* a link counts as found by trial even when nothing at all was tried, as long as nothing earlier already stood for the answer. *Example:* someone who has never seen a pendulum writes a formula on a napkin and says "this stands for the pendulum"; it counts as an explanation. A student copying it from a textbook still does not. *Seems to go against* S41 Q2: "No, not if just declared".

**C8.** *In one sentence:* a worked-out link counts as worked out only if the explanation it leaned on while being worked out itself passes the tests. *Example:* a navigator works out a course with a method that fails on the open sea; her course still comes out right for the harbour, but on this reading it counts as merely declared. (Only on the reading that "worked out" asks about the explanation the working used.) On the same reading, an explanation of your weathervane worked out with a claim about another part of the vane that does not pass the tests stops being an explanation. *Seems to go against*, on that reading, S41 Q2: "No, not if just declared" (her link was worked out), and S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained".

**C11.** *In one sentence:* something whose answer is simply written into one part can pass the tests but is not an explanation. *Example:* "it is red because it is red" passes but does not count. Your two-part sign stays an explanation on the reading that a part is "written in" only if it alone gives the answer everywhere asked, and stops being one on the other readings. *Seems to go against* S45: "Yes, take the test out"; and, on those readings, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation."

**C12.** *In one sentence:* anything that passes the tests is an explanation, even if its link to the thing was only declared. *Example:* the student who copies a working pendulum formula and writes "this stands for the pendulum" has an explanation. *Seems to go against* S41 Q2: "No, not if just declared".

**C15.** *In one sentence:* a question counts only if what it describes could be built in just one way; if several different set-ups would behave as described, nothing answers it. *Example:* "why is this lamp on at night and off at noon?" asked of any lamp that behaves so, when many different circuits do: on this reading no explanation of the lamp counts. On the reading where your sign is described only by what it shows (red on Mondays, blue on Tuesdays), several different signs would do that, so neither your two-part explanation nor any other explains it; the same for the weathervane. *Seems to go against*, on that reading, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation.", and S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained".

**C16.** *In one sentence:* a link found by trying things counts as found only if the trying says what the link was built from; otherwise it counts as simply declared. *Example:* a gardener tries many watering schedules and keeps the one that works, but never writes down what it is made of; on this reading her schedule is merely declared, and explains nothing. An explanation of your sign or your weathervane reached by trying and keeping what worked, with nothing stated about how it was built, would stop being an explanation. *Seems to go against* S41 Q2: "No, not if just declared" (the question you answered set a link "simply declared" against one "found by trial or worked out") [Xd2]; and, for such a history, S44: "In either case, it is an explanation." and S41 Q15: "Yes, it can be explained".
